naevus.definition: A small spot on the skin made of a cluster of pigment cells. Most moles are harmless, but a new or changing mole should be checked, because melanoma can start in or look like one.

eruptive-naevi.definition: Many new moles that appear within a short time, sometimes weeks. They have been linked to some medicines, illnesses and tanning peptides.

dysplastic-naevus.definition: A mole whose cells look abnormal under the microscope. It is not cancer, but people with many of them have a higher risk of melanoma.

melanin.definition: The dark pigment that colours skin, hair and eyes. Pigment cells make it and pass it to the skin cells around them; it absorbs part of the sun's ultraviolet light.

tyrosinase.definition: The enzyme in pigment cells that starts turning the amino acid tyrosine into melanin.

melanoma-in-situ.definition: The earliest stage of melanoma: the cancer cells are still only in the top layer of the skin. Removing it by surgery usually cures it.

mc3r.definition: One of the five melanocortin receptors. It is found mainly in the brain, where it helps control appetite and energy use.

pres.definition: Swelling in the back of the brain, often linked to swings in blood pressure. It can cause headache, fits and other brain symptoms, and in most people it gets better.

renal-infarction.definition: Death of part of a kidney because its blood supply is suddenly blocked, usually by a clot. It often causes sudden pain in the side or back.

sympathomimetic-toxicity.definition: Poisoning that over-activates the body's fight-or-flight system: a racing heart, high blood pressure, sweating, wide pupils, shaking and agitation.

erythropoietic-protoporphyria.definition: A rare inherited disease in which a substance builds up in the skin and reacts to light. Even short exposure to light can cause severe burning pain.

dermoscopy.definition: Looking at a mole through a lit magnifying lens, often with photos, so a doctor can see patterns that the eye alone misses and compare them over time.

conditioned-taste-aversion.definition: When an animal learns to avoid a taste it had just before feeling ill. Researchers use it as a sign that a drug makes animals feel sick.

circumventricular-organs.definition: Small areas of the brain where the blood-brain barrier is open, so substances in the blood can reach brain cells there.

blood-brain-barrier.definition: The tight wall of cells around the brain's blood vessels. It keeps most large molecules, including most peptides, out of the brain.

vitiligo.definition: A condition in which the skin loses its pigment cells in patches, so those areas turn white.

sun-protection-factor.definition: A number that says how much longer protected skin can stay in the sun before it burns, compared with unprotected skin. SPF 2 means about twice as long.

creatine-kinase.definition: A protein inside muscle cells. When muscle is damaged it leaks into the blood, so a blood test for it shows muscle damage.

ultraviolet-light.definition: Light from the sun and from sunbeds that the eye cannot see. UVB burns the skin; UVA goes deeper. Both can damage the DNA in skin cells and lead to skin cancer.

amide-end.definition: How a peptide chain finishes. Most chains end in an acid group (a free acid); in some it is replaced by a small cap called an amide. Melanotan II has an amide end; bremelanotide has a free acid end.

spinal-fluid.definition: The clear fluid around the brain and spinal cord. In animal studies, drugs are sometimes injected into it to reach the nerves directly.

dermatologist.definition: A doctor who specialises in the skin, hair and nails, including moles and skin cancer.

debarment.definition: A US ban on a person working for any company that has, or is seeking, approval for a medicine, imposed by the FDA after certain crimes.
